utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. My associates noticed you mentioned the S. Hase elementary school. In Bijeljina they think this is a bit of a joke because there is a primary school there, Marko Filipovic, Zikica Jovanica, Zikica Jovanica Spanac, and Hamza Hamzic. There is another secondary school centre called Alija Aliagic, but there is no elementary school by the name of S. Hase in the Bijeljina area at all. The citizens of Bijeljina are watching this, are attending these proceedings. So do you say that a school named S. Hase actually exists? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Well, from this place I cannot check anything out. Perhaps it is in the vicinity of Bijeljina and so the witness said that it belongs to Bijeljina. But I'm sure that such a school does exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You then talk about a prison. There's no prison let alone a school, let alone a prison. So how can anything then exist? Then you have an agricultural school listed here. Can you name one single Muslim who was detained in an agricultural school? The agricultural school worked as an agricultural school.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: It probably exists. I'm sure it exists, or rather, I'm sure that documents exist about that particular locality and the individuals. As I say, everything was compiled on the basis of statements in the dossiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were Muslims in the school but just as teachers, the teaching staff of the school, not as detainees or prisoners. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you have Osman Velagic's house in Janja. That's the next one. Not a single Muslim was ever imprisoned in Janja. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that the house existed as a place of detention. Persons who were detained in the house testified to this. They were mistreated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you quote a name? Can you give us the name of somebody who was detained there at all?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Don't expect me to give you names, Mr. Milosevic. I have tried not to do that because I wasn't -- I was only -- I only prepared my report but without any specifics. So I can't give you a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you also say that the police station in Janja was a prison. My information tells me that the entire police station has three rooms, one for the duty officer, one for the chief and one for -- as a cloakroom, and that in Janja throughout that time in the police force there were a number of Muslims working there as policemen. Nobody was detained or held there. Perhaps somebody was taken into custody, an offender of some kind who had committed some kind of offence or crime. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I know that people were taken into custody, detained there, and mistreated. And when you're talking about camps, schools, police station buildings were used, and other facilities as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Malesevic, you're saying all this. You're giving us some general information and general facilities used as camps. I am being specific and asking you about the fifteen camps in Bijeljina that you have listed, and nobody in Bijeljina knows about them except for this Batkovici collection centre, that one Batkovici collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Well, our members -- our witnesses know more about that and can give you more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When we come to the Batkovici centre, my associates have collected information about that, and that information speaks of the following - and please confirm this or deny it - that in that collection centre of Batkovici, the International Red Cross had a continuous presence there and it was through this collection centre that persons were taken for exchanges and that nobody from that centre went amiss in any way. Do you have any information or facts that anybody suffered a fate otherwise in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. 3.800 persons passed through Batkovici, according to our facts and figures and this was an agricultural estate. Terrible, horrendous crimes took place there. Prisoners were forced to drink their own urine and other people's urine. They had to do strenuous physical labour, they had to beat each other, they were forced to beat each other, and there was terrible abuse and mistreatment. Predominantly the detainees were men. They were taken off to dig trenches, communicating trenches, to make up a live shield, human shields. Other inmates were brought to Batkovici as well. The International Red Cross Committee did visit and tour the camp but it wasn't there all the time, it wasn't present all the time. And many detainees were hidden away when these ICRC visits took place. So any who passed through Batkovic were not registered by the International Committee of the Red Cross at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any proof about what you're saying now, what you're claiming? Because according to the information amassed by my associates, everybody was registered and there are reports and minutes about each individual case, and I think the opposite side, the other side over there has those documents as well.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have a lost documents when it comes to the Batkovici camp and the terrible horrendous things that people were put through there. The fact is that the International Red Cross did visit it, that's why mass killings did not take place here -- there, but persons were kept without food until the point of hunger. People were beaten, their ears were cut off, they were abused horrendously and maltreated in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not enter into the details any more. But my information tells me that nobody was killed in the camp, that they were all registered, that the Red Cross did visit the camp and that via this collection centre, in fact, it was prisoners of war who were exchanged. And you're saying that none of that is right. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The witness has given her evidence. She says there was mistreatment there, and no point going over that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about a report on places of detention, real ones and otherwise, toured by the KEBS commission in Bosnia-Herzegovina from the 30th of August until the 3rd of September, 1992, places where persons were allegedly detained? And you have the OSCE report on that.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. Not fully at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They visited a total of 21 centres. That was the number they were told existed according to the report, and I will tender the report. They visited -- in seven centres the data proved to be false because there were no people in those seven centres, which leaves us with 14 centres; 21 minus 7. And we have the Muslim part of the Ripac village ten kilometres from Bihac. Bihac, Manjaca, Trnopolje, the police station in Livno, the school in Livno, the village of Rascani, the prison in Mostar, Sarajevo Viktor Bubanj, and then the ones where nothing was found I won't bother to read out. Then there is Bileca, Susica, Batkovic, Konjic. And they have here that Bihac was held by the Muslims, that Viktor Bubanj Sarajevo was also under Muslim control, that the sports hall in Konjic was under Muslim control, that Celebici and the others were under Muslim control. So on this list of theirs, of the 14 where there were some persons, I've enumerated several under Muslim control. This is an OSCE report, although the OSCE report was compiled in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, Ripacki Logor was under the control of the Serbs, not the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Bihac now and by Bihac, nearby Bihac. That was Serbian controlled. That's what it says. In Bihac it was the Muslims that had control. Livno, Croatia. In the school, the Croats. In Rascani, Croats. Mostar, Croats. Viktor Bubanj Sarajevo, Muslim control. In the sports hall in Konjic, Muslim control. And in Celebici, also Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So are you aware of these camps, the ones I've just read out, because you say you have nothing about that, and here we have an OSCE report dated 1992. So from the 30th of August to the 3rd of September, 1992 they toured these different localities to ascertain what existed there.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I do know those camps and the places stipulated, but this is an incomplete OSCE report. We have been doing research work for seven years now, and we uncover something new all the time. So I can't actually say that the report is incorrect, but it is incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So incomplete as it is, it does contain information about several Muslim camps, whereas you say you have no information about Muslim camps.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I did not say that. I said that we do have registered and recorded camps under Bosniak control, and they are dealt with in the same way, because we look at the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we have members regardless of ethnic and religious affiliation, and we look at camps as camps. Detainees are detainees regardless of their ethnic affiliation, religious affiliation, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a moment ago for the Muslim victims you said "ours," and then you said if the Serbs provide data, then we'll have a complete report. So you don't consider the Serbs to be yours, your own.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to our alliance. Our alliance of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which implies a multinational alliance. But as you are presenting the kind of data that we don't have, I think it would be a good idea to coordinate all this data to see where we are stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that you don't even have the kind of information that the OSCE commission ascertained?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: As I say, the data is incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I do believe that it is incomplete too but even that incomplete data does contain information. For example, in point 16 here, as Zvornik is referred to - and you spoke about Zvornik and a camp there a moment ago - and here it says no proof. The number of detainees found: Zero. Only 20 Serb refugees were found there. That's what it says here. And that was on the 2nd of September, 1992, the OSCE mission visiting Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, but up until September they were either all killed, dispersed, exchanged, or whatever, and I can well believe that no Bosniaks were found there. I can accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the accused says he's going to submit this report. Probably the sooner it's submitted, so that we can look at it, the better. It's difficult for the witness to be dealing with sentences taken out of context if we don't know what the context is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Have you got it, Mr. Milosevic? Have you got any copies for us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll give you copies straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mrs. Malesevic, that it was said that there was a camp for Muslims in Serbia too?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that that mission came to look into the matter because somebody had provided them with erroneous information that in the mines of Aleksinac there was allegedly a camp? Do you know about that incident?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know they went to check this out, but that place did exist, I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it says here the Aleksinac mine in Serbia and there is no proof, zero detainees and no evidence or proof of detainees, the 3rd of September, 1992. There was never any camp in Serbia at all.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to remind you about Zivovica, Metrovi Polje [phoen], Sremska Mitrovica, Uzice. Those were all localities where the Bosniaks were taken and detained. As for the OSCE report that they didn't find anybody there at that time, I can agree with that. Perhaps at the time they went there there was indeed nobody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, look at the people of Aleksinac. They would be able to tell you best whether there was a camp in the Aleksinac mine at all. You can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ask the people, the coal mine there. Do you think that if that were true, it could be hidden? A truth like that could be hidden?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the public didn't know about many places and I do think that is possible, that it could have been concealed from the public. And I think that the Serbs in Serbia did not know about localities of that kind. That is possible as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, Mrs. Malesevic, that the authorities of the Republika Srpska told me that apart from the prisoner of war centres, there were no camps at all on the territory of Republika Srpska or in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Well, except for the prisoner of war centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, where the prisoners of war were held, such as those that were taken prisoner in combat. The Serbs on the Muslim side or the Muslims on the Serb side or the Croats on the Muslim side, the Muslims on the Croatian side, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that that's what they told you, however, the information was kept confidential and hidden from the public and they still are hidden from the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it would be very advantageous for you, Mrs. Malesevic, to have the truth out, to reveal the truth so that we know about all the camps.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my ultimate goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't leave that impression on me with the information you provided us with as to that being your goal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In terms of time, Mr. Milosevic, you have another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes is too little, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You speak of Trnopolje. Do you know that Trnopolje was a refugee centre that was open, that people came in and out of? That was where the forgery was made, where that lady, I think her name is Ms. Marshall, I think the film was shown, this forgery --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You're not putting this claim, this allegation which has been dealt with frequently. You're not putting it to this witness. You can call your evidence about it, but there have been several court cases already which have dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I would like to tender this OSCE report. And before you take it, you have here also an UNPROFOR proposal for the exchange of prisoners signed by Abudllah Razek, Brigade-General of Sarajevo, sector commander of UNPROFOR, Serbs captured by Bosnian armed forces in Tarcin, 700; in Posevici 150; in Hrasnica, 23. And also the Bosniaks captured by Serb forces in Luka, 57; at Ilidza, 7; at Hadzici, 600. So this was written by Brigadier General Abudllah Razek, commander of the Sarajevo sector. It was an UNPROFOR proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just a moment. You're not giving evidence. We'll look at those documents. Which is the OSCE report? We've got one -- since it's not in English. We have here UNPROFOR. We've got that. We can see it with a list of camps. Just a moment. Just a moment. Let me finish. Then you've also given us what appears to be a totally unattributed list. Now, what is this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a part of the OSCE report of that date, written on that document. If necessary to get hold of the original document, we can get hold of it. It is in the OSCE archives. There's no question about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to return the partial document. We will call for the entire document. Have you -- perhaps you can help us with it, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know yet if I have it. If I do, I'll produce it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll probably know better at the end of the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If not, Mr. Milosevic, you can get it for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're checking for it now, apparently.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll obtain it for you. There will be no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we might do, just so that we don't get confused later, is mark that extract for identification as a Defence exhibit, give that the first number and then we'll give the UNPROFOR document the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the partial OSCE report will be marked for identification as Defence Exhibit 111. And the UNPROFOR will be Defence Exhibit 112.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Malesevic, I assume that you cooperate with the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have here a report and information. The data is prisoners of war which are being regularly visited by the International Committee for the Red Cross in Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated the 14th of May, 1993. And then the location is given, the number of prisoners, and the date of the last visit. They are being regularly visited. Under the supervision of Bosnian Croats in Livno, Mostar, Orasje, Rascani, Slavonski Brod, Kaonik, and Prozor. Now, my question is regarding those under the supervision of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it says here, those are the ones you don't know about. And this is the 14th of May, 1993, Breza, Bihac, Hraznica, Igman, Mraziste, Kladusa, Konjic, Ramiz Sarcin, Sarajevo, Stupari, Sarajevo Centre, Tarcin, Pazaric, Tesanj, Tuzla, Visoko, Zenica. And then under supervision of the Bosnian Serbs, Banja Luka, Tunjice, this is a regular prison for decades, Batkovic that we've spoken about. The hospital in Bijeljina where one is registered. Doboj, Kotor Varos, Kula, Kula Butmir Sarajevo, and then a small camp at Banja Luka, no prisoners. Visegrad, no prisoners. Zvornik, no prisoners; and Zasavica, again there are some. So do you know anything about these camps which, according to the report, this report, were visited by the International Committee for the Red Cross that were held by Muslims? Breza, Bihac, Hrasnica, Igman, Mraziste, Kladusa, Konjic, Ramiz, Sarcin, Sarajevo, Stupari Sarajevo Centre, Tarcin, Pazaric, Tesanj, Tuzla, Visoko, Zenica, do you know anything about them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Before you do, let the witness see the document. She can't possibly comment on it without seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The heading is "Prisoners of war that are being regularly visited by the International Committee of the Red Cross in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: This report of the International Committee is dated 1993, where, according to our records, many camps under Serbian control were closed, which means in 1993 the number of camps was significantly reduced. As for the camps under Bosnian control, of course we are familiar with some of them. But for your information, I can tell you that the camp in Velika Kladusa was thoroughly investigated and processed. It was under the control of Fikret Abdic. I personally participated. We have plenty of evidence for that. We have evidence for Tarcin and Konjic as well. However, many of the detainees listed here are not on our list. Maybe they're not in Bosnia. Maybe they haven't contacted us. I must say again that we compile all our reports on the basis of authentic statements of witnesses. We don't rely too much on international bodies because really we wish to check out everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the camp at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in that location it was Serbs in the first place who were detained?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that Alija Izetbegovic, on the 8th of October, 1992, visited the camp at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And had you heard that on that day members of the Green Berets took an oath of allegiance in front of them while the Serb detainees were in manholes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is going well beyond the witness's evidence. Now, Mr. Milosevic, you've got about another two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how many Serbs, former detainees, became members of your alliance, Ms. Malesevic?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Just now I'm unable to say with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know of a place called Dretelj close to Capljina?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in that location the authorities also formed a camp for Serbs, exclusively civilian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of Dretelj as a camp held by Croats and in which both Serbs and Bosniaks were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what if Croats held it; then it's not relevant?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We have it on our records.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does your Alliance know who Ahmet Makitan, known as Maks, father's name Omer, from Stolac is?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Edib Buljubasic is, a former JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about this? You didn't learn from any witnesses how many tortures were committed by these two men? Let me just give you some examples. Abuse, rapes, killings of Serbs in Dretelj, in that particular camp that you're familiar with. You know of the camp, but you don't know anything about what happened there nor who were the perpetrators. You know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I can't go into those details now because I haven't prepared myself for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know Srecko Herceg and Blazo Kraljevic? Have you heard of them?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you know about the Dretelj camp, then you must know that they were the managers of those camps, the wardens of those camps. So you don't know anything about that. And Alliance, your Alliance, in view of Article 11 which envisages among its tasks and assignments the filing of charges against those who were abused by your members. Have any charges been filed against someone who killed, massacred, or abused Serbs in those camps?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: We are just preparing material for such criminal proceedings, and very shortly we will be filing charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the barracks of the former JNA, known as the 27th of July, in Bihac from 1994 to 1996 was transformed into a camp in which members of the VRS were mostly detained?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were camps for prisoners of war. But we are mainly concerned with civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as an alliance, since Article 17 of your Statute says that you will represent the interests of detainees and their families which are alleged to still be in aggressor camps, did you also represent the interests of the families of any Serb who was killed as a result of beatings, torture in one of those camps, roasted on the spit, bodily parts cut off? Did you file charges or did you represent the interests of family members of any one of them?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do represent the interests of all those members who applied to us. I can't remember that we had an example of a Serb detainee contacting us. I can't claim that there weren't any, but I can't recollect any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can have two more questions, Mr. Milosevic, and then your time is up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does your Alliance have information that anyone from the Republic of Serbia or in the Republic of Serbia founded a single prison or camp for persons from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do have some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which information? Please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Sljivovica, Mitrovo Polje, Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sremska Mitrovica is a regular prison.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to which Bosniaks from Bosnia-Herzegovina were illegally taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to Mitrovo Polje in 1995 in which a whole brigade was housed which fled to avoid extermination in Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact that there were only males, but elementary human rights were violated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Malesevic, do you know that I received that brigade, allowed it to cross the Drina to save their lives? There was 840 of them, and that on that same day they were visited --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This goes way beyond her evidence. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, testimony of this kind which turns Serbs into monsters cannot be cross-examined in such a brief period of time, because this is a pile of lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is by way of comment, not a proper observation. You've had your chance to cross-examine. You were told that there would be a limit on time. If you have an application, you have some more information you want to put, more detailed information, we will consider it in due course, but meanwhile, Mr. Tapuskovic to cross-examine. We haven't yet -- just one moment. I'm sorry, Mr. Tapuskovic. We haven't yet dealt with the Red Cross document. Mr. Milosevic, you referred to a Red Cross report. Again, it appears here in the form of a faxed list. What we don't have is the -- have you got the rest of the report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can provide it. Unfortunately, I have here very limited -- it would be putting it mildly to say modest possibilities, but I can provide the documents in their entirety. But Ms. Malesevic has seen this document. It is a report of the Red Cross, and it is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We will exhibit it in this way: We will mark it for identification, give it the next exhibit number, and then in due course you can produce the original, I mean the whole report, in which case we will give it a full exhibit number. But for the moment we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will be marked for identification as Defence Exhibit 113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Malesevic, I have very limited time for the cross-examination, and I should like to try to address only two points, if I can, and to explain to Their Honours a few things. The first relates to Article 1 of the Statute of the Association of Camp Inmates of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is tab 1, Exhibit 104 [as interpreted]. Article 1. It says: "The Association of Camp Inmates of Bosnia and Herzegovina (hereinafter the Association) is a voluntary non-partisan association of citizens, former inmates who accept its program and this Statute..." So primarily of citizens; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it was adopted on the 25th of August, 2001. This is the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. 2005 [as interpreted], I'm sorry, which existed for five years.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: No. The statute was adopted in 1996 and amendments were made in 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself: On the 25th of August 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in any case, Bosnia-Herzegovina existed already for many years in the form in which exists today.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So I would like to know whether this is a statute that was approved also by the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: As you see in our programme aims, we wish to act throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. It has been certified by the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but has it been approved by Republika Srpska? And I'm asking this because of something that is contained in the Statute that is reference to aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina. Has Republika Srpska approved the contents of this Statute?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. We were registered by the Ministry of Justice. Whether they gave their approval or not, but the Association has the status of a legal entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you because it is hard to include in a Statute of this kind something that still has to be proven, especially as this is a state consisting of three entities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: She said, "I can't say anything about that." Very well, can you explain for Their Honours tab 5, referring to killings and torture and physical mistreatment. Here you mentioned a whole series of forms of killings and torture and physical abuse. Also, in the last tab, we saw photographs which have been seen many times already here in various places. I would like to know, if you could explain to Their Honours, first regarding torture and physical abuse. This was reported by survivors, obviously. For example, under 21, tearing -- tearing off genitals of detainees by criminals. Do you have a photograph of such people?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, sir, but how can you expect photographs of such crimes? We have an authentic witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But wouldn't it be logical if there were survivors for us -- to show us a photograph of such a horrific crime?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: If -- even if I had a photograph, I wouldn't be able to present it without permission of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If you can't do for that, then for number 30. Something detainees against wooden and glass objects. Do you have photographs of that?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't have any material evidence, any photograph or any of these things listed from 16 to 44 here?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Material evidence are the consequences that are still visible on the bodies of former detainees, and a host of witnesses who were watching this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the witnesses watching this. I'm asking you about these people who survived and complained to you of the horrific torture they were subjected to. Why don't you have a single photograph to corroborate what they experienced?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: We don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few points arising. Just dealing with the last point of Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say you have no photographs of injuries. We've seen some photographs of injuries already, but you have no photographs of injuries of the particular categories of abuse that he referred to?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any particular reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, when crimes of this kind were committed, there was no filming, or rather, the detainees were not in a position to take photos, because this was all done far from the public eyes and it is only the inmates that can testify to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Insofar as the inmates would be describing injuries inflicted on them as individuals, any reason why we haven't got photographs of those?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: That is possible, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is possible there are some photographs of the injuries that they sustained?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which brings me to the next point. Brings me to the next point: Does your documentation include medical reports where medical reports would be appropriate, or not? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are medical findings and reports attached to the majority of cases. However, many, when they left the camps, were not able to seek medical assistance straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused --

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: We do have a certain number of medical reports, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused asked you a number of questions suggesting that detention centres simply didn't operate as detention centres. Now Mr. Tapuskovic has apparently challenged certain of the allegations of torture and physical abuse. Your records are clearly substantial and voluminous, but would it be possible for you to return to those records and to search them in respect of these particular challenged locations or challenged injuries and to find records that sustain your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You haven't turned all your records, very substantial as they would be, over to the OTP of the ICTY, and I'm not for one second suggesting that you should do that, but is there any reason of confidentiality or similar why, having identified those particular records about detention centres and injuries, any particular reason why you shouldn't make them available to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, all the documents that I place at the disposal of the Tribunal I will have to ask acquiescence from our members once again, but I assume that there is a portion of those documents that cannot be handed over to the Tribunal, and this refers to the rape of women and, as a result, those women bore children. So I don't think it would be a good idea if data of that kind were to be presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Malesevic, there will be no detailed questions about that. I'm only concerned with the very particular suggestions that have been put to you by the accused and now by Mr. Tapuskovic. If you find documents dealing with those particular allegations, and we'll list them for you before you leave, I hope, will you be in a position to find and to produce to the Chamber documents that support what you've said?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first thing I'd ask is that when she leaves, Mr. Agha will extract from LiveNote a list of all the challenged locations and challenged acts of torture. We can send those with the witness and she can then take whatever time is necessary and send us a package of materials and we will provide them to the Chamber and to the accused. If that would be appropriate. If seems to me it arises from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What we have in mind is this: That the Prosecution should be able to produce the evidence. Of course, if need be, we may have to ask the witness to come back to deal with it in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to make things quite clear: The request made by Mr. Nice just now is absolutely unfeasible, because she cannot obtain a list of the challenged elements of her own testimony when I have not had time myself to challenge the elements in her testimony. What she can get is just a list of what during this short space of time I did succeed in challenging and contesting. And as I have been limited in time, you can imagine what other things I could still challenge and contest. So the expression "all the challenged material" is quite inappropriate. I challenge the entire testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will deal with those parts on which there were detailed challenges. That material can be provided and we'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Malesevic, you just heard the accused say that he challenges the totality of your testimony, and you will have heard him earlier raise "pile of lies." I think it's a suggestion that you've been lying to this Chamber. Now, you've given an account of how individual alleged inmates and victims record their histories for your Alliance, and you've identified how they have some limited benefits arising from membership of the Alliance and how they sometimes have to be checked out.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there any other benefit passing to them as individuals, to the municipal or other local associations, or to you as an officer of this Alliance preparing these records? Do you get anything out of it?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: For what we do, and we do it for a large number of people both in the field and in the Alliance, nobody reaps any benefit from it. Our work is almost on a volunteer basis. Nor do our members enjoy any kind of rights. The sole motive there is truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the accused pressed you about Serbs. You said yes, there were Serbs in the associations but you didn't have the particular statistics of ethnic composition. Given your Alliance's multi-ethnic principles, is there any reason to break down those who claim to have suffered in this way on grounds of ethnicity or not?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think there is, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused has placed before us two pages in your own language that you I don't think have seen of the OSCE report. I mean, haven't seen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could see that and the UNPROFOR page, just before she leaves court just to see if she has any comments on them in their original form and see indeed if she recognises them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let her see them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And while we're coming to you, Mrs. Malesevic, do you know anything about the methodology of the alleged OSCE report one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I must say that I don't know about the methodology, the methodology they used in their work. However, this is the 3rd of September. According to our information, many camps were already closed by that date when we're speaking about Eastern Bosnia. I have never seen this document before. I'm looking at it for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that was the OSCE extract, so described.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if you look at the other document that has come to you. Just see if you've seen this one before. It may be the Red Cross document.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: No. I haven't seen this document either before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Cast your eyes down and see if there's any comment you want to make on it.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: What they say, Tarcin here, we do have records of Tarcin, and we know that it was a camp where there were detainees. In addition to Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs were there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No other comment?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then finally this: Has there been any question of Serbs applying to register their interest in your Alliance being rejected on grounds of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: No, not for ethnicity. Nobody was refused on those grounds. The only thing that might have happened was that the material wasn't complete. But we are a multi-ethnic Alliance, so there would be no reason to reject any claims or requests from those quarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, are there associations that are Serb based or Serb-dominated perhaps because they exist in Serb-dominated areas?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. According to our information, quite recently an association was set up in the RS of survived detainees, and we're preparing to enter into contact with them so that we can work together, get the material that they have and so on. We had earlier contact previously with another association of missing persons and detainees. They encompassed those persons killed, detainees, missing persons. This has been separated now, and it is an Association of Detainees separately, and we have good cooperation with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all I ask of this witness, subject to the fact that she will be asked to bring documents or to find documents and send them to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Malesevic, that concludes your evidence for the time being. What we're going to do is to ask you to produce some documents on the matters you were questioned about. It may be that we will have to ask you at some future date to return to give evidence about those documents, but meanwhile, thank you for coming to the Tribunal, and you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be convenient, while the witness is departing, to deal with one or two interlocutory matters that we've been asked to rule on. One matter is the Witness Zana Baca. I may have mispronounced that. We gave leave that the witness should be substituted for another witness last week. The question which we're now asked is whether she may give her evidence under Rule 92 bis. We think that appropriate. She will be coming to give evidence anyway and will be cross-examined. The witness -- the amici asked us to extend time in one particular case dealing with the admission of transcripts. We will grant that as asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are asked to deal with some protective measures for a witness -- witnesses. It's the application of the 5th of March. Since we're in open session, I won't mention the names, but there are three witnesses, the application of the 5th of March. We shall grant that as asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that concludes those matters. Shall we start the next witness? Yes. We've got ten minutes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not been informed of any changes to the order of witnesses, although before the break you did give instructions that I should be informed on time about the order of witnesses. On my list I have Zana Baca, and not Djordjevic who is going to be next. On my list he comes after her. So I should just like you to take note of that, that not even your instructions were respected and abided by by the opposite party, that is to say, to let me know on time as to the list and sequence of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Our list dated the 3rd of March makes it plain that he is to be next, Mr. Djordjevic is to be next.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I usually receive the order of witnesses. The last one that I received says Baca Zana, followed by Djordjevic and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got the 27th of February and that also gives Mr. Djordjevic as next. I don't know what date you've got. It sounds as though you're dealing with an earlier document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be that the accused is -- has in mind a conversation that Ms. Dicklich, who sits next to me, had with his associates where at some stage she said there was a possibility that, for administrative reasons, Baca and Djordjevic would have to be reversed but in fact -- and the associates were invited to alert the accused to that possibility, but in the event, the list is as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll hear his evidence next. How long do you think you will be with him in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm anxious to try to finish him this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To finish him today?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may not, but I'm anxious to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You will have this afternoon to prepare your cross-examination of this witness. Let me deal with one other matter, and that is that Dr. Ranta I think is due on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That being so, her evidence, since she has been fixed for a particular day, will have to be interposed. So we will hear Dr. Ranta on Wednesday, whatever the state of the evidence, and any other witness will have to be dealt with around her evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Grateful for that. And I don't know if the Court's formed a provisional or indeed final view as to how her evidence should be dealt with and what should be the order of the questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I thought we'd made it plain. If we haven't, we will deal with it by way of her producing her -- any statement, that we will in due course have examination -- any questions by the Bench, examination by the Prosecution, examination by the accused and the amici, and then any other questions by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Milosevic, to explain that, that when Dr. Ranta comes, we will first of all have the Prosecution giving cross-examining or examining. We will then -- you will then follow, and then it will be the amici, and that will conclude her evidence. The Bench will ask questions either at the beginning or the end according to the determination of the Bench itself. I think by this time we're really up to the break. Yes. We might as well break. We will break a bit early and have 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We're having a witness sworn. Yes. Let the witness be sworn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, what is it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I can provide the entirety of the report of the International Red Cross dated the 14th of May, 1993, of which I gave you only one page. And secondly, could you please tell me how much time I will have for witness Helena Ranta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We haven't yet worked out times. Why? Are you thinking you may need a longer time than usual?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I just like to be informed how much time I will have as she's planned for Wednesday so that I have an idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have in mind an hour. You'd have an hour to cross-examine her. But let's go on with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness, as the Court may remember, was originally listed with a pseudonym. He made it plain, as I revealed on an earlier occasion, that once he'd received the waiver he required, he was content to give evidence fully openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My surname is Djordjevic, my first name Milosav.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour will also recall that the witness's statement has been the subject of an application that part of it be admitted under the provisions of Rule 92 bis, an application that was granted, and amongst the various paragraphs that are to be admitted under 92 bis, paragraph 1, paragraphs 22 to 25, paragraph 29, and then paragraphs 47 through to 70 and indeed 71. The first paragraph -- sorry. May the statement and what's called the 92 bis package now be produced and given its exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Prosecutor's Exhibit 405.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness produces several exhibits which come collected together in a file. May they also be produced immediately and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibits for Mr. Djordjevic will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 406.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You are, I think, a retired general; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And from the extended curriculum vitae which is before the Chamber in written form, we extract that on the 20th of October, 1991, you were appointed head of the Coordination Group at the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia for SAO Krajina, and you started to work there for General Tomislav Simovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He being the Minister of Defence for Serbia, you holding that position until -- a fairly short period of time, until the 22nd of December of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Serbian Ministry of Defence was established, as you understand it and can assist us if necessary, according to various laws and was based on the then-existing Secretariat for People's Defence, the SNO of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You would say that the legal basis for the establishment of the Ministry of Defence can be found in a number of laws, and you've listed them as follows: The 1990 Serbian constitution, the 1974 SFRY constitution, the 1982 SFRY All People's Defence law, the 1984 Serbian All People's Defence law, and the 1991 Serbian All People's Defence law?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In addition, you refer to the rules of internal organisation and systemisation of work within the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was adopted by the government of Serbia in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally, you've been able to bring to The Hague one further document which is the 1984 Law of Defence of the Republic of Serbia, which is tab 1 in our exhibit, the number of which I've already forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 406. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 406, tab 1. And if we can just have a look at that very briefly, very briefly. If we turn to the 4th page of 10, as it appears in the bottom right-hand corner, we see that Article 111 is under the sub-heading Republic Secretariat for People's Defence and that it goes to say: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "The Republic Secretariat for People's Defence, within its domain, and beside the affairs which conducts according to the general regulations on administrative bodies, conducts the following administrative affairs ..." and then it lists them. And at number 13 on page 6 of 10, at paragraph 13: "Organises, monitors and coordinates preparation and training of working people and citizens for All People's Defence in cases of immediate war, threat, at war, and in other special situations." Page 7 of 10, paragraph 24. The body carries out certain affairs for the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, and the system is listed there. And you would also draw our attention over the page to page 8 of 10, paragraph 29: "In cooperation with the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, the appropriate army commands, organs, and the JNA, it participates in ensuring the reinforcement of armed forces and other needs of All People's Defence in organising and conducting of training exercises; it makes and coordinates plans for the Defence ... takes part in choosing war locations." Perhaps paragraph 30, third line: "The Republic Secretariat for National Defence, in case of imminent war danger, in case of war, as well as in other states of emergency ..." and sets out what it does. And that's, I think, all I need ask from you by way of a very general survey of that one additional Statute. So these Statues and Rules, as you understand it, provide a basis for the Serbian Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Quite so. But the new Law of People's Defence of the Republic of Serbia of 1991 eliminated some of those tasks and reduced them in relation to the contents of the 1984 law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence of the -- we'll look very briefly at the control of the Ministry of Defence and the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence, the SSNO. Was the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia part of the Serb government; and if so, to whom did it answer?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could I have a table shown, because it would be easier to explain. But I can do it without also.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In that event, let's look at tab 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that go on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And making it, General, if you would, please, as simple as possible, because complexity may not be required. We see here the government of the Republic of Serbia in the centre, with the Prime Minister identified, and then the Ministry of Defence below it with its minister identified. We'll come to the coordination office in due course. Question: To whom did the Ministry of Defence answer?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the first place, the Ministry of Defence is accountable to the government of the Republic due to the very fact that the Minister of Defence is a member of the government. At the same time, both the government and the Ministry of Defence are accountable for their work to the National Assembly. So each Minister, in addition to being accountable to the government, is also accountable to the Assembly of Serbia. But for certain activities within the competence of the president of the Republic, the Minister of Defence is also accountable to the president of the Republic as he is to the government. As for the Federal Secretariat for National Defence and its relationship with the Ministry of Defence of the Republic, this horizontal line pointing left and right means that these ministries cooperate, that is the SSNO and the Ministry of Defence. And this top arrow indicates that for certain activities, the Federal Secretariat for National Defence is superior to the Ministry of Defence of Serbia, primarily when the Presidency of the SFRY transfers some of its competencies to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. And then the SSNO has this superior role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Remind us, if you would, of SSNO. What is it an abbreviation for?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Federal Secretariat for People's Defence. I hope. Your Honour, if we simply note on this chart that there is a coordination office within the Ministry of Defence, we can then look at the next chart, tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a chart, General, that identifies the principal tasks of the Ministry of Defence. The tasks of the ministry, I think you say, are dealt with in the 1984 law that we looked at very briefly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we look at this diagram, which is quite busy but simplified for us by colour, can you help us, please, with the -- the charts -- sorry, with the tasks as identified by the various different coloured chains? Was there something to do with the monitoring and preparation of the population for the defence of the Republic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we have shown here the tasks of the coordination group as a working body attached to the Ministry of Defence of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's deal with -- yes. My error. Let's go back one stage then and just deal with the main tasks as you would describe them before we look at this particular document. The main tasks of the ministry itself, what do you say they are? Forget the chart for the time being. What do you say the main tasks of the ministry were?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The main tasks of the Ministry of Defence were to monitor, initiate, prepare, and guide the overall defence preparations of the civilian structures of the society of Serbia, to cooperate with the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, the commands of army districts, and the republican staff for National Defence in the preparation and organisation of all people's resistance, not regarding the use of armed forces. And a special task which the Federal Secretariat for National Defence transferred to the Ministry of Defence for Serbia was to collect information regarding the condition, preparation, and availability of staff for the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Autonomous Province of Krajina, or Krajina, all three which joined to form the Serbian Republic of Krajina. So this was done because the commands of the military districts were overburdened with their operative tasks of commanding the armed forces. So it was thought appropriate for the Minister of Defence of Serbia to do a part of those tasks on behalf of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the Ministry of Defence get involved in military planning at the strategic level or was it more limited, do you say, in its function?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. The Ministry of Defence of Serbia did not take part at all in operative planning, the use of the armed forces at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did it give assistance to the Territorial Defence or to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That it did. It did assist it through mobilisation, preparations of personnel, providing supplies, but not within the direct competencies of the ministry but in cooperation with the commands of the armed forces and the Federal Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it involved at all in the training of the Territorial Defence of Serbia, or indeed in the SAO Krajina's Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, in the event, hear something about the man Vasiljkovic, whether he was engaged in training?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragan Vasiljkovic, or Captain Dragan, as he was known, did once visit the Ministry of Defence. When I met him in the corridor, I didn't speak to him, but I heard from Minister Simovic that he had requested that he be approved the use of so-called Bubanj Potok, which is a training centre, a shooting range and a training centre for soldiers which was under the control of the command of the defence of the city of Belgrade, that is, under the JNA. And through some sort of an arrangement reached between the command of the army district and the Ministry of Defence - I don't know who else participated - he was given this permission for Captain Dragan to organise a training centre in Bubanj Potok, which is 16 or 17 kilometres from the centre of the city. However, as far as I have been informed, literally three men came to attend that training course, two from Krajina and one from Belgrade or Serbia, so that that course never took place there. I didn't inquire into that, nor was it my duty to concern myself with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the Serb Ministry of Defence have relations with the Serb Ministry of the Interior in which information was exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you recall as an example one particular meeting involving Simovic, the Minister, and Aleksandar Vasiljevic and Zoran Sokolovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Also about Radmilo Bogdanovic. In 1988, did he become Minister of Internal Affairs of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did he resign technically?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was after the large-scale demonstrations in Belgrade in March 1991 or shortly after that. I don't know the exact date. He submitted a request for resignation to the Assembly and it was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was replaced, as we know, by Sokolovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in fact did Bogdanovic retain any position, any influence in the ministry thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogdanovic did not have any position in the ministry, any official position in the ministry any longer. However, as his successor was a person, according to certain beliefs of people who had contact with him, had not been properly prepared to take over that position in -- behind the scenes, amongst ourselves we referred to Minister Bogdanovic as a shadow minister. In other words, that they were closely cooperating and Bogdanovic was probably assisting him, but I don't have any specific evidence to corroborate that or any document to that effect but that was the general belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the closeness or otherwise of the relationship, if any, between the Sokolovic and the accused? What did you discover about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall from the party work, that is when the League of Communists of Serbia was still in existence, Mr. Sokolovic was the secretary of the Central Committee, and at the time Mr. Milosevic was president of the Central Committee. So quite naturally, they had close, direct relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard of the Ministry for Ties with Serbs outside of Serbia. Did the ministry for which you were working, the Ministry of Defence, have relations with that other ministry?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. But I did not attend any meetings of either Ministers. There were a large number of refugees that had come in from Croatia, from Krajina, who came to see us, the Defence Ministry and my own coordinating group, and they were intermediaries as was the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry for Ties with Serbs outside Serbia. We helped them find accommodation, to see to their well-being and so on. I apologise, but there's a clause, let me just say, in the new constitution, the constitution of today, that the Ministry for Relations with Serbs outside Serbia has as one of its tasks to assist them in maintaining their independence, autonomous character, their human rights and so on and so forth. So those ties emanate from those provisions and that kind of situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was there a similar level of contact between the Ministry of Defence and the agency for immigration led by Radmilo Crncevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It would be more correct to say -- to call it the Matica Iseljenika, not for immigration but the matrix. And Mr. Radmilo Crncevic at that time was the president of this Matica association. And then there were ties and cooperations along the lines I mentioned earlier; the Defence Ministry and the Matica for refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've told us of the general functions of the ministry, and now I get to the chart that I put on the overhead projector too early, tab 3. Were you on appointment in October 1991 made head of something called the coordination group for SAOs within the Serbian Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Throughout that period until December 1991, did you remain an active-duty JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Typically, would your appointment to this task have required a decree of the SFRY Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It would have been typical had a general been appointed to a set post, and my case could be considered in that regard. But why wasn't this done? According to the law on national defence of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Presidency appoints generals, the Federal Secretary for National Defence appoints Colonels and lower ranking officers, the commanders of the Territorial Defence officers up until the rank of colonel for their own units and formations. However, this was not typical. It wasn't a typical appointment as a permanent organ and part of the ministry, the body of the ministry, because it had a department for military matters, for defence and protection and other departments. This was a working body, an ad hoc body. So I was sent to work there and not appointed permanently, because my active service was to have expired by the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did General Krstic, head of the personnel sector at the SSNO, have anything to do with getting you to do this job?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. Prosecutor. I submitted a written request in mid-October after all the events that came to pass in Croatia and the general attacks on the barracks, which is where one of my officers, one-time officer was executed within the frameworks of a barracks that was taken over in Bjelovar. As I had passed over my duties to somebody else, there was no sense in me remaining in my position of retiree. And therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... just for a moment, General. I just wanted to know, and I think you said yes, did General Krstic have something to do with your appointment; and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did he have to do with it?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: He did in the sense that I tabled a written request that my decree in pensioning me off be rescinded, postponed until the end of the war. After that, General Krstic called me up on the telephone and told me that the decree would not be changed. Several -- I do apologise, but several days after that conversation, we had another conversation over the phone, and he told me that there was the option of me going to the JNA command, a corps of some kind somewhere, but that the decision was revised and I was sent to the Ministry of Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So it was --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: -- of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- Krstic appointing you to this --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He was the head of the personnel sector. And we can't say explicitly that he appointed me. All he did was to convey to me on the basis of my request to the Supreme Command that it was decided that I go to the Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes. The ministry of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Coordination Group of which you were now the head for the SAOs within the Serbian -- within the ministry, did it act in some way as an intermediary between the SSNO and the Ministry of Defence and the local Territorial Defences and the SAOs in Krajina, Western Slavonia, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many people worked in the Coordination Group?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact figure. There was an order to that effect, an internal order, actually, but it was between seven and ten persons, officers, mostly colonels by rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All, or all bar secretarial, military?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All were members of the military, members of the JNA, either retired officers or officers who had already handed over their affairs and were about to retire --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was the --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: -- like myself. More or less in the same position as myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was your office, physical office, initially located in the main building of the Serbian Ministry of Defence, subsequently moving to another part of the city of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think there may have been a plan to divide the Coordination Group according to geographical division of the SAOs, but that was never implemented.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one small passage that the witness would only be in a position to give in private session. There's one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The colour-coded chart, tab 3, now on the overhead projector, shows, I think, the six main tasks of the Coordination Group. Can you interpret the chart for us, General, colour by colour, but starting with which ones you regard as the most important, the most major tasks, if there is such a distinction.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There was no major distinction, but our emphasis was on the following tasks: I'm going to point from top to bottom, moving downwards. The realisation of requests for officers, that is to say officer cadres for the Territorial Defence of SAO Krajina and responding to those requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the blue line.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back. Yes. I'll go back to an explanation. Just let me enumerate. The next was request for logistical support for Krajina; the quartermaster section, technical, materiel, and so on. The next request was assistance in constituting Territorial Defence units, organising them not for combat but according to the systematisation, what belongs to whom and so on. And finally, in the bottom right-hand corner, preparation of the staffs of SAO Krajina to take in the UN forces, because there are intimations that they would be arriving to monitor the cease-fire in Krajina, or rather, in Croatia. But let me go back to the first request.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've temporarily overlooked salary payment and money, but we'll come to that at the top of the chart in due course. Very well, request for officers, the blue --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, yes. That was a slip. We'll go back to that. But the number one task, or first from the top, is to -- or, rather, from the TO staff of Krajina, they asked us to send them officers, and we didn't have enough of those officers. As we did not have officers available in my direct group or ministry, what we had to do was to send on the requests to the Personnel Department, that is to say, General Krstic and his officers, and other commands who had officers available, if I can say had a surplus of cadres, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The blue passage pointing up to SSNO goes like that and then up to SSNO, and then the line shows, does it, officers being provided direct by the SSNO across the top to those bodies that had requested them.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And we were also simultaneously informed that that had been carried out.
